title: Is AI Ruining the Web? Fake News, Stolen Books, and the 2016 Nostalgia Trend
description: In this issue, we discuss how the rapid development of artificial intelligence and algorithms has changed the Internet beyond recognition, and why society has begun to resist these changes.

All these pictures from a decade ago, old Snapchat filters, and this phrase, 2026 is the new 2016. And yeah, it feels like a fun, simple throwback, but trust me, there's something way deeper going on here. We're going to unpack why everyone is so obsessed with the internet of 2016 all of a sudden. So, this isn't just, you know, a couple of people posting old photos. This is a huge full-blown cultural moment. It started bubbling up late last year and then just exploded at the start of 2026. We're talking millions of people digging through their camera rolls, all looking for a very specific vibe from a very specific time. I mean, this slide just takes you right back, doesn't it? Remember that summer of Pokémon Go when we were all just outside wandering around chasing digital creatures on our phones? or the mannequin challenge where everyone would just freeze in place for the camera. The music, the filters, it honestly feels like a whole different world. And the memories are so so specific. We're not just feeling nostalgic for the 2010s in general. No, it's about this stuff, the puppy dog filter, the glory days of Vine right before it died. The first season of Stranger Things. For a whole generation of people, this right here was the internet. But that's the million-dollar question, right? Why this year? Out of all the years in the last decade, why has 2016 become this digital monument? It's not just a simple 10-year nostalgia cycle. The answer actually says a lot about how we feel about the internet we have today. So, it turns out this whole trend is actually a symptom of a much more deliberate movement. People are actively trying to rewind the clock on internet culture to pull off what's being called a meme reset. They aren't just remembering 2016. They're trying to bring its whole vibe back. You know, for a lot of people, 2016 feels like the last moment of a certain kind of digital innocence. It was right before the online world changed, before misinformation got so out of control. And this is the big one, before artificial intelligence started to completely flood our feeds. And here it is pretty much spelled out. The Great Meme Reset is a conscious push back against what a lot of people call brain rot. That endless scroll of loweffort, weirdly hypnotic content. And it's especially a rebellion against the title wave of AI. It's a call to go back to a simpler, more human, more homemade online culture. And really, it all boils down to this. A recent report from Goodrebels put it perfectly. People just miss when social media felt spontaneous and genuinely entertaining. They miss when the whole point was just to share goofy stuff with your friends, not to build a brand. Okay, so to really understand why everyone wants to go back, we have to talk about what they're running from. And that brings us to the rise of something that's being called AI slop. Take a good look at this number. 1.3 billion. According to Tik Tok's own data, that is the number of videos on their platform that are officially labeled as AI generated. And as insane as that sounds, that's just the tip of the iceberg. I mean, those are only the videos that people bothered to label. The real number of AI generated videos, images, and text posts out there is probably way, way higher, and it's being used for everything from spamming for engagement to spreading straight up lies. And this this is exactly what people are reacting to. This weird, uncanny, slightly off, lowquality content is what's getting called slop. It feels dehumanized because, well, it is. It's just an endless stream of digital noise that's drowning out actual human creativity. And this isn't just about weird memes and cringy videos anymore. The whole issue has blown up into a massive economic and legal fight. This is where that fun nostalgic trend collides headon with some very serious highstakes global policy. And just check out the language being used here. A recent report from the UK Parliament is not mincing words at all. It describes AI models being trained on creative work without permission or payment as a clear and present danger. That's pretty intense. And here's why governments are starting to take this so seriously. Just look at the money. The UK's creative industries, that's music, film, books, all of it. They added 124 billion pounds to the economy. That's more than 10 times the value of their entire AI sector. So the fear is that sacrificing the creative industries for the sake of AI is, as the report puts it, a poor bet. So what we have now is this massive fork in the road. And not just for the UK, but for the whole world. Different countries are starting to pick sides and they're sketching out two very, very different futures for how AI and human creativity are going to coexist. And this slide really breaks it down. On one side, you've got the path the UK and the EU are taking, a licensing first model. Basically, if an AI company wants to train its model on your art, music, or books, it has to get your permission and pay you for it. Simple enough. But on the other side, a proposal from Russia suggests the complete opposite. Letting developers use copyrighted material for free without consent. All to speed up AI development as fast as possible. So, let's bring this all back home. The memes, the throwback pictures, the longing for 2016. It's all pointing back to this one single fundamental question that we're all dealing with right now, whether we realize it or not. At the end of the day, this whole 2026 is the new 2016 thing is so much more than a hashtag. It's a collective gut level reaction to an internet that feels more and more fake and automated. It's a deep yearning for a time when the web just felt more human, more creative, and honestly, more fun. And that really leaves us with this final thought. Every time we hit post on our favorite 2016 memory, we're actually taking part in this huge debate about what comes next. The choice between a future where creators get paid or one where they don't is going to define our digital world for decades. So, as we're looking back to find some comfort, the real question is what kind of internet are we building for the future?

AI and Water are more connected than most people realize. As artificial intelligence continues to expand, the data centres that power it are using millions of litres of water every day to stay cool. This invisible demand is creating ripple effects across our freshwater systems, and ultimately, our ocean.

 In this episode, Andrew Lewin uncovers how AI’s explosive growth is reshaping global water use. From groundwater depletion and saltwater intrusion near coastal data hubs to desalination discharges harming marine life, the story goes far beyond servers and code. He breaks down how indirect energy use from AI contributes to ocean warming and acidification, revealing that every digital action has a hidden aquatic cost.

 Andrew also explores innovative solutions—from recycled and non-potable cooling systems to closed-loop designs that dramatically reduce water loss. With growing global demand for AI, he highlights the urgent need for transparency, accountability, and smarter policy design to protect both freshwater and marine environments.
